Recent findings suggest that shiba Inu (SHIB) gained 5.96% over the past 24 hours and traded at $0.0000038 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap, as talk of a December "Santa rally" returned to the crypto market. Still, SHIB is down 8.86% over the past seven days, and the token has lost 18.5% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

Last week, SHIB dropped to $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021.

The hopes for a Santa rally come after Goldman Sachs analysts noted last week that most of the December gains on the stock market usually come after Dec. 15. SHIB's own December history, however, reveals that the Santa rally came for the token once in five years.

Sources indicate that according to CryptoRank, SHIB lost 29.5% and 13.5% in December of 2021 and 2022, respectively. In December of 2023, the token gained 24.6%. In December of 2024 and 2025, SHIB lost 21% and 17.6%, respectively.

SHIB's median December return is -17.6%, and its average December return is -11.4%, according to CryptoRank data.

It has been revealed that the green December of 2023 came after SHIB gained 6.04% in October and 6.62% in November of that year, according to CryptoRank. In 2026, SHIB lost 18.6% in October, and November is also in the red so far.

The Goldman note, titled "GS Flow of Funds: Chopsgiving," came from Gail Hafif, Brian Garrett and Lee Coppersmith, who looked at S&P 500 data going back to 1928. According to the note, the index usually gains 1.1% from mid-November to early December and then gives back about two-thirds of that gain by mid-December, and around 80% of the full 2.4% gain comes after Dec. 14-15.

Sources indicate that since 1990, the S&P 500 has risen after Dec. 15 in 27 of 36 years, according to Goldman.

It has been revealed that the Goldman team called these figures a historical map. In the years when the VIX volatility index was above 18 in the middle of November, the S&P 500 gained 1.34% on average, and the index ended the year higher in 59% of cases, according to the note. According to Goldman, the VIX was above that level in mid-November of this year as well.

Goldman also said that retail investors have been buying significant tech and chip stocks. Large funds and systematic traders have been cutting their positions, according to the note.

The Stock Trader's Almanac counts the last five trading days of December and the first two trading days of January as the Santa Claus rally. This season, the window will open on Dec. 24 and close on Jan. 5.

In the window that ended on Jan. 5, 2026, the S&P 500 declined 0.11%, according to the Almanac. "Santa was a no-show for the third year in a row," the Almanac wrote. Before that, the S&P 500 also ended the Santa Claus rally windows of 2023 and 2024 lower.

  • Industry observers note that meta’s upcoming teen restrictions, set to take effect by late February, could meaningfully curb endless scrolling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 25, 2026 at 8:21 am.

Industry observers note that meta’s upcoming teen restrictions, set to take effect by late February, could meaningfully curb endless scrolling. A new study suggests they probably won’t.

That’s because the restrictions, which are part of a settlement between Meta and dozens of attorneys general, including Washington’s, apply only to Instagram and Facebook. They leave out Snapchat, TikTok and Google-owned YouTube.

In a recent development, “The simple workaround right now is that you just switch platforms, and we already know that teens are on three to four platforms on average,” noted Dr. Dimitri Christakis, a principal investigator at the Center for Child Health, Behavior and Development at Seattle Children’s.

Christakis led research published Wednesday showing Instagram and Facebook accounted for roughly 20% of total daily social media use for youth. So when the restrictions kick in, teens could just shift to other platforms.

Industry observers note that the rules establish a two-hour daily limit combined across Instagram and Facebook, restrict access to content from midnight to 6 a.m., and mute most school-hour push notifications. Parents can adjust the protections, and direct messaging is exempt.

If the same limits were applied across the five most popular platforms, that could make a dent in teen usage, according to the research letter in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

In an analysis of recorded app activity from 1,803 adolescent Android owners, the researchers estimated:.

The study has no way of knowing how teens will respond to the restrictions or the impacts on their health. It simply estimates how much previously recorded activity would fall under the rules.

Industry observers note that the researchers disclosed ties to social media litigation. Christakis reported paid legal consulting work, including for Washington’s attorney general, and co-author Lauren Hale of Stony Brook University reported fees for serving as an expert witness. The third author is Yihong Zhao of Columbia University.

Despite the limited benefits of the coming restrictions, Christakis said they’re a “step in the right direction.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Let’s say it’s an incremental improvement. It’s clearly not going to be enough by itself because of what our study found,” he mentioned. “But these are the right kinds of restrictions. We need to make them universal, and we need to enforce them.”.

Meta, not surprisingly, is in favor of having the restrictions apply industry wide.

When the settlement was announced in August the company issued a statement saying that “ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative.”.

Meta called on others to do the same: “For meaningful progress to happen, we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this newly introduced standard…”.

Recent findings suggest that the agreement resolves claims by 48 states, Washington, D.C., and U.S. territories that Meta designed addictive platforms and failed to protect young people, among other allegations. Meta did not admit wrongdoing.

In addition to the safety changes, Meta agreed to pay participating governments up to $17.1 billion over a decade, according to Washington’s attorney general. Washington will receive at least $237 million and could receive nearly $339 million.

The higher settlement is unlocked only if TikTok and YouTube adopt similar protections and make payments of their own, according to Meta. If that happens, additional restrictions kick in, curbing access on all the platforms from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m.

Those additional hours are significant. The researchers found nearly as much use between 10 p.m. and midnight as during the entire midnight-to-6-a.m. window covered by the initial limits.

In a recent development, whether the other companies will follow remains unclear. All five social media platforms are named in additional legal challenges alleging harm to youth, Reuters reported, including suits filed by individuals, school districts and municipalities.

In September, TikTok reached its first settlement in a state-led case, agreeing to teen usage restrictions in Alabama and a payment of at least $100 million, according to Reuters. YouTube CEO Neal Mohan, meanwhile, dismissed joining Meta’s agreement and emphasized his company’s own safety efforts, CNN reported.

In a recent development, christakis noted both time spent on social media and the platforms’ features can exacerbate problems involving sleep, mental health, body image and attention. He hopes the growing body of research translates into action.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m not a legislator, and I’m not an advocate. I’m a scientist that’s really trying to make sure that we apply science in the best interests of our children’s health,” he mentioned. “And in this space, in particular, we haven’t been doing that.”.

Recent findings suggest that most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

Industry observers note that according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to fresh institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The manufacturer indicates R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

Sources indicate that the project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the firm, cost nothing.

According to recent reports, the reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Sources indicate that ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as new rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

In a recent development, the risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

According to recent reports, the details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

According to recent reports, "Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let people redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

According to recent reports, in the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

It has been revealed that eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent manufacturer, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU introduced earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

According to recent reports, the bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on manufacturer disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

In a recent development, for everyday owners, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

It has been revealed that the trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

‘Positive Charge’ season finale: What we learned chasing climate solutions across eight episodes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:10 amNovember 25, 2026 at 9:11 am.
  • Editor’s note: GeekWire reporter Lisa Stiffler, who covers climate and sustainability, co-hosts the Positive Charge podcast with producer Laura Scott.
  • It has been revealed that we went inside a fusion lab in Everett, a jet fuel plant in Moses Lake and a factory in British Columbia giving old EV batteries a second life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:10 amNovember 25, 2026 at 9:11 am.

Editor’s note: GeekWire reporter Lisa Stiffler, who covers climate and sustainability, co-hosts the Positive Charge podcast with producer Laura Scott.

It has been revealed that we went inside a fusion lab in Everett, a jet fuel plant in Moses Lake and a factory in British Columbia giving old EV batteries a second life. We tasted plant-based chicken nuggets at 9 a.m. and stepped into a shipping container in Tacoma that destroys “forever chemicals.”.

Over eight episodes, the inaugural season of the Positive Charge podcast from GeekWire went across the Pacific Northwest (and beyond) in search of promising climate and sustainability technologies to help humanity dig our way out of some pretty dire environmental straits.

While the challenge is huge — a warming planet, increased use of fossil fuels, toxic chemicals in our food and water — there are wide-ranging solutions out there, and many are taking hold.

On this episode, GeekWire co-founder Todd Bishop sits down with producer Laura Scott and me, the hosts of Positive Charge, to look back on the season. We explore the themes that emerged across the episodes, savor some highlights and even get a little emotional when discussing the question of whether all of it left us more hopeful about the planet.

Going behind the scenes. At Helion Energy in Everett, we got a sneak peek of a miniaturized fusion test device that was cordoned off and still under construction. To see it, we walked behind a huge plastic curtain, which Laura memorably compared to walking into the Costco dairy section.

It has been revealed that our podcast on alternative proteins went inside Rebellyous Foods, a startup manufacturing plant-based chicken nuggets being served in U.S. schools, as well as some medical and correctional facilities. We were offered a plate of the nuggets — which we scarfed down, despite the tour taking place first thing in the morning.

“My biggest regret of the whole season,” Laura noted, “is that we did not take Rebellyous up on their offer to send us home with those chicken nuggets because you cannot buy them in stores.”.

The importance of large, committed customers. A lot of these technologies are expensive propositions, from R&D to prototypes to scaling. “Having a willing and able corporate buyer is something that can really spark the innovation to happen,” Todd observed.

That includes Microsoft’s agreement to buy power from Helion, purchase agreements for sustainable aviation fuel from Twelve and Montana Renewables, and Redwood Materials‘ deal to supply used EV batteries to power a data center for Crusoe. Rebellyous built its business on school lunch programs.

The essential role of organizations coming together collectively to support new sustainable technologies was a key message of a New York Climate Week panel, where I interviewed Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, and Jason Knauf, CEO of The Earthshot Prize.

In a recent development, we discussed the fact that when customers commit, it unlocks investments to scale production. That in turn lowers costs for everything from faux nuggets to cleaner jet fuel.

AI is driving the money. The data centers behind the AI boom are often cast as a threat to tech companies’ climate goals. In several episodes, they were also a reason for money to flow into clean energy.

“There’s so much money going into environmental solutions because of data centers,” Laura noted. “It’s a catalyst for funding. It’s a catalyst for fusion.”.

There’s money to be made. While many sustainability entrepreneurs are fundamentally mission-driven, they’re also focused on the fiscal bottom line and so are venture capitalists.

Recent findings suggest that at Pacific Northwest Climate Week, Laura was struck by how enthusiastic investors are about the space, and not only because they want to save the planet. They’re “entirely self-interested,” she mentioned, “and that’s what gave me hope.”.

Sources indicate that PNW is a sustainability hub. In each episode of Positive Charge, we toured a Pacific Northwest startup, plus we interviewed related companies outside the area and sector experts.

The local companies included Helion and Zap Energy in Everett, Aquagga in Tacoma, Sedron Technologies in Sedro-Woolley, Twelve in Moses Lake, Rebellyous in Seattle and Moment Energy in British Columbia.

The range of topics reinforced the region’s standing as a hub for sustainable tech, including batteries, fusion, aviation, environmental cleanup, and even potentially overlooked fields, such as end-of-life services.

Recent findings suggest that laura’s unexpected favorite episode was about startups offering human composting as a green alternative to burial or cremation, and Todd ranked it a close second (his No. 1 was EV battery reuse).

Industry observers note that seattle is home to Recompose — the first U.S. organization to offer the service after its founder, Katrina Spade, spearheaded the effort in 2019 to make the practice legal. Since then, human composting startups Return Home and Earth Funeral have also rolled out in the Seattle area.

After exploring all of these technologies and talking to entrepreneurs, investors and leaders in the space, Todd asked if we were more or less hopeful for the planet.

Industry observers note that “Definitely more hopeful,” Laura said. “I didn’t expect to feel more hopeful, though. I expected to feel about the same, or maybe a little bit worse.”.

But seeing the financial case for these solutions helped shift her thinking. One example is Sedron, which is treating sewage waste with a technology that destroys PFAS forever chemicals and also generates enough clean electricity that the excess can be sold to others. Laura was impressed by the opportunity to do right by the environment while creating revenue.

Industry observers note that I hover between hope and anxiety. But after years of covering these complications, I appreciated a sentiment shared by Earthshot finalist Franco Rodríguez Viau, CEO and co-founder of Satellites on Fire, who stated he needs to do everything he can to tackle climate change, whether or not humanity succeeds in reaching its goals.

According to recent reports, that’s how I feel about covering climate. As I mentioned on the show, I don’t know if I feel hopeful, “but I can’t feel indifferent. I have to show up and do this.”.

Positive Charge is a GeekWire podcast sponsored by Amazon Sustainability.

The past weeks have seen the broad crypto ETF market face consistent withdrawals from investors, causing Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Solana, and others to record steady outflows since October.

While the negative trend has continued, Solana has just taken over the leadership in the broad ETF market after recording its first inflow in a while.

Latest data from SosoValue indicates that while Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP ETFs have continued to struggle with consistent weekly outflows, Solana has just beaten the trend after it finally ended a six-week streak of consecutive weekly outflows.

Notably, the data shows that Solana spot ETFs have recorded a net inflow of $4.38 million over the week.

Although the net amount of capital received by the ETFs appears decent, it is significant considering the growing crypto market weakness.

While this marks an end to the Solana ETFs' six-week outflow streak, this is the first positive weekly performance they have recorded since October 9.

Further data demonstrates that Bitcoin spot ETFs suffered the largest withdrawals as investors pulled out about $1.79 billion during the same period.

The negative trend also extended to the Ethereum ETF market as the funds posted a total of $314.17 million in net outflows following the consistent selling pressure.

In addition to this, the XRP spot ETFs were not spared, as the funds recorded $11.11 million in weekly outflows, leaving Solana as the only one among the four major crypto ETFs to finish the week on a positive note.

Sources indicate that as the asset continues to plummet, market experts are sharing their data-driven analysis, with one such being Bloomberg’s Mike McGlone. The market analyst believes  that Bitcoin could follow the same pattern observed during the NFT market crash and fall to as low as $10,000.

The Bloomberg Intelligence senior commodity strategist Mike McGlone declared on Sunday that “the everything bubble is bursting,” arguing that broad declines across major assets are already under way after years of aggressive money creation.

In the first half of his post, McGlone said the Bitcoin and crypto bear market since October 2025 “may be a guide of what to expect in most markets, particularly the US stock market, gold, metals, commodities and US Treasury bond yields; they’re all going down. It’s simply overdue reversion.”.

He expects sharp short-covering rallies that “typically gotta keep false hope alive to feed the bear,” comparing many cryptocurrencies to the collapse of NFTs and warning that tokens tracking nothing could approach zero. Bitcoin, he added, may find a “good gravity-pull pivot” near $10,000 to clear speculative excess.

In the second half of his post, McGlone argued that the strong annual gains previously seen in Bitcoin, natural gas, gold, silver and other commodities would reverse and spread weakness into the broader stock market, potentially leaving the S&P 500 with its third annual decline since 2009.

It has been revealed that he anticipates significant drawdowns that began from early October highs, lower prices for crude oil and copper, a shift by the Federal Reserve toward easing, and a normal post-inflation period of deflation as US housing peaks. Elevated mortgage rates and Treasury yields, he stated, will later be viewed as an opportunity for investors, with the year more likely to finish in volatility than calm.

“Substantial green 2026 annual candles in Bitcoin, US natural gas, gold, silver, platinum, palladium, iron ore, nickel, lead, corn, copper, the Nasdaq….will gain contagion with the S&P 500 Total Return ending the year with its third down year since 2009. A 50% drawdown likely started from the Oct. 6 high, a year after Bitcoin’s peak and about 9-months after gold’s top. Crude oil back toward $40. Copper Under $5…” he wrote.

Etzioni on AI: 18 ways to use AI this Thanksgiving

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that here are 18 creative ways to use AI this Thanksgiving.
  • Apps like Flighty (start with free tier) use machine learning to predict whether your flight will leave on time and why it might not.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:17 amNovember 25, 2026 at 10:16 am.

Sources indicate that here are 18 creative ways to use AI this Thanksgiving. Some save you time in the kitchen or at the airport, and others aim to make the meal more fun. The don’ts at the end could save your turkey, and my very last suggestion is perhaps the best.

Flight delay forecasting. Apps like Flighty (start with free tier) use machine learning to predict whether your flight will leave on time and why it might not.

Recent findings suggest that cancellation playbook drafted in advance. Have the backup flights and a rebooking script ready ahead of time, so a cancellation means consulting your AI instead of starting from scratch.

Sources indicate that airport pickup routing. Five relatives land at different times at two airports, and AI works out who drives whom. It can even send a polite request on your behalf.

A personal travel agent. Vayo (free, private beta), a latest Seattle startup co-founded by my friend Mike Fridgen, connects to your inbox and pulls in your flight, hotel and restaurant confirmations. It keeps an eye on them for price drops and changes.

Industry observers note that oven Tetris. Give it your oven’s size, every dish’s temperature and the serving time. It works backward to a minute-by-minute schedule and flags the conflicts.

Industry observers note that decoding grandma’s recipe card. Photograph the card and have AI modernize it under one rule: it never invents quantities. “A pinch” stays “a pinch.” “un poco” or “ein bissl” may be translated, but not changed.

Recent findings suggest that reconstructing a lost dish. Several relatives describe a dish a late grandparent made. AI triangulates a recipe, you cook test versions, and the family votes on which one tastes right.

Industry observers note that pairing from the wines on hand. AI picks from bottles you actually own, and those brought over by guests, dish by dish, instead of a generic list. Last-minute fun!

Potluck dispatcher. One AI thread collects RSVPs and dish claims so you don’t end up with four green bean casseroles.

It has been revealed that trivia built from your own family’s facts. ChatGPT can now run it as a playable game, with answer buttons and a running score inside the conversation.

AI-prepped grandparent interview. Feed the AI what you already know and have it draft questions about the gaps. Record it, and afterward AI turns the transcript into a short illustrated booklet that’s in the mail by Christmas.

Industry observers note that angry Uncle rehearsal. Karin Tamerius, a political psychiatrist, built the Angry Uncle Bot, and it still runs in ChatGPT. A coach asks for your matter and your stance. You set the uncle’s temper from Annoyed to Apoplectic and choose whether he’s drunk or sober, and the coach critiques each reply before he answers.

Live interpreter for multilingual families. Put ChatGPT’s voice mode (paid prepares) in the middle of the table so the great-aunt who only speaks Hebrew or Spanish is part of the conversation instead of watching it.

Sources indicate that friday leftover remix. Photograph the fridge and get a menu that makes Friday’s leftovers feel like a new meal.

In a recent development, specific thank-you notes. Each note names what that person actually brought or stated.

Photo triage. AI picks the best 20 of 400 photos and captions them in the family’s inside-joke voice.

In a recent development, “We missed you” letter for someone who wasn’t at the table. AI drafts it from the stories told at dinner.

Recent findings suggest that black Friday skeptic. Before you buy, check Google’s price insights, which tells you whether a price is high, low or typical for the past three months. Last year, 36% of Black Friday items showed no savings over their prices a few weeks earlier. Better yet, set a price track and let Google’s agent buy the item at eligible U.S. stores when it hits your number, after you confirm.

I consider myself an OG Black Friday skeptic. Back in 2011, I told the Latest York Times (gift link) that after crunching the price data at my startup Decide.com, the lowest electronics prices usually came in early December, not on Black Friday.

Recent findings suggest that don’t trust an AI turkey recipe on its own. Back in 2022, when the Fresh York Times cooked a Thanksgiving from GPT-3 recipes, the turkey recipe called for one garlic clove for a 12-pound bird and no butter or oil. It came out dry and flavorless.

Don’t take a chatbot’s word on an airline’s rules. Air Canada’s chatbot told a grieving passenger he could claim a bereavement discount after he flew. The real policy remarked no, and he had to take the airline to a tribunal to collect $812 (Canadian). Check the airline’s own policy page, and screenshot what the bot tells you.

According to recent reports, don’t click on the deal of the century. Scammers now use AI to make fake shopping sites look legitimate, and the number of fake sites jumped 250% last holiday season, according to NordVPN. Type the retailer’s address yourself.

Sources indicate that don’t try to win the family argument with AI-fetched facts. Even the creator of Angry Uncle Bot states that bombarding your uncle with facts only makes him angrier. Ask questions and listen instead.

Here’s another option: give technology a rest.

Unplug from your devices and from AI, and have an AI-free, 100% human Thanksgiving.

Veteran trader Peter Brandt has softened the tone of his recent Bitcoin warnings and mentioned on X that the cryptocurrency held at the level it needed to hold after its drop to $55,150 over the weekend.

"Bitcoin held exactly where it had to hold -- for now anyway, but perhaps for more than now," Brandt wrote on Monday.

It has been revealed that brandt also shared a monthly chart of Bitcoin together with the post. The chart goes back to 2018, and Brandt marked on it the same patterns that he had already pointed to in previous years. According to the chart, the price of Bitcoin was back above $63,000 at the time of the post and stood at $63,338.

Recent findings suggest that on Saturday, Bitcoin fell as low as $55,150. It was the lowest price of the cryptocurrency since September 2024, and before that, the lowest price of Bitcoin in 2026 was $57,718 on July 1, according to Coinbase.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 15, Brandt posted a weekly chart with a possible head-and-shoulders top and stated that, if the pattern proves valid, Bitcoin's October 2025 record of about $126,000 may not be surpassed in his lifetime. Two days before that, on Nov. 13, Bitcoin dropped below $70,000 for the first time since August.

Brandt has also pointed to the history of Bitcoin's bull market cycles more than once. Late last year, he posted a chart showing that each of Bitcoin's five major bull runs began after drawdowns of 75% or more, and he wrote that if the decline carried to $50,000, "the next bull market cycle should carry to $200k to $250K.".

In April, Brandt mentioned that Bitcoin could form an "investable low" in September or October 2026. According to Brandt, this low may or may not go below the February low near $60,000, and the next cycle peak could land between $300,000 and $500,000 in September or October 2029 if the four-year cycle continues to hold.

"Real bottom will not occur until October 2026," Brandt mentioned in an interview in February.

The latest Brandt post comes amid a rally in U.S. tech stocks on Monday. Earlier that day, Nvidia declared that its board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, chief executive officer and board member, effective immediately.

Industry observers note that according to the Nvidia announcement, the board received input from senior levels of the U.S. government before the decision, and it is confident that Huang's return "poses no national security risk." Shares of Nvidia surged 33% after the news, according to CNBC.

It has been revealed that bitcoin went up together with tech stocks and briefly climbed above $64,000 on Monday. Before the Nvidia news, Bitcoin had already recovered from the Saturday low to around $61,500.

Industry observers note that huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12. On Nov. 17, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said on the company's earnings call that the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.".

Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3.
  • Recent findings suggest that the most key words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made.
  • On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

Recent findings suggest that the most key words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division noted it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It has been revealed that it also mentioned it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

It has been revealed that early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

It has been revealed that the staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

Recent findings suggest that this is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

In a recent development, legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

Industry observers note that A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself indicates the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

According to recent reports, in practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

Sources indicate that for a firm, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

According to recent reports, that sequence matters. The interpretation states what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

Recent findings suggest that the practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

It has been revealed that for now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite the sharp fall in the cryptocurrency market, Michael Saylor-led Strategy has not stopped its Bitcoin (BTC) buying spree, as it picked up 457 BTC worth around $29.6 million.

The firm's recent purchase comes as the leading cryptocurrency has been struggling to rebound from the heavy sell-off that recently dragged it to a two-plus-year low.

The latest data from Strategy's SEC filing reveals that the firm has bought 457 Bitcoin at an average price of $64,898 per coin.

The new purchase brings Strategy’s Bitcoin holdings to around 851,305 BTC, which accounts for over 4% of the cryptocurrency's maximum supply of 21 million coins.

The firm has now spent around $64.23 billion to build its Bitcoin holdings at an average price of $75,446 per Bitcoin.

It is worth noting that Strategy has been buying BTC at gradually decreasing prices as the cryptocurrency market continues to bleed heavily.

It has been revealed that on Nov. 2, the firm unveiled that it had bought 811 BTC, worth around $65.5 million, at an average price of $80,846 per Bitcoin.

A week later, on Nov. 9, Strategy announced the purchase of 1,036 BTC worth $81.9 million at an average price of $79,012.

The firm’s Bitcoin purchase a week later, on Nov. 16, was relatively smaller at 485 BTC, worth $33.4 million, with an average price of $68,887.

Sources indicate that the new 457 BTC purchase continues this pattern. The latest Strategy purchase was made at an almost 20% lower price than the firm’s Nov. 2 acquisition.

Overall, the firm has made four weekly purchases, scooping up around 2,789 BTC worth $210.4 million.

Industry observers note that however, these purchases have been much smaller than before. The latest $29.6 million purchase is almost 64% lower than the $81.9 million purchase unveiled just two weeks ago.

Although Saylor is doubling down on Bitcoin, Strategy’s massive holdings in the cryptocurrency are underwater as the market has been struggling to regain its footing.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 21, Bitcoin hit a low of around $55,130, its lowest level since September 2024, before rebounding above $61,000.

The firm’s recent purchases have helped reduce its overall average Bitcoin acquisition cost, but the drop has not been that significant.

For example, with the latest purchase, the average cost of the firm’s Bitcoin holdings dropped from $75,452 to around $75,446, a decline of just $6 per Bitcoin.

At the same time, the firm has also been putting a lot of resources into supporting its preferred securities.

In the latest reporting period, Strategy sold around 1.93 million common shares, raising net proceeds of $176.7 million.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 25, 2026 at 4:46 pmNovember 25, 2026 at 4:48 pm.

The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to send up to a million satellites into orbit for its Starmind data-processing network.

In a news release, the FCC touted today’s decision as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space” and echoed the high-flown language that SpaceX used to describe the network in its application 10 months ago.

“It promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization — one that can harness the full power of the sun,” the agency noted.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr noted the plan “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”.

Carr signaled that he was all in on the Trump administration’s support for rapid data center expansion, despite a growing backlash that figured in this month’s midterm elections. He mentioned that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership” in artificial intelligence.

“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” Carr remarked.

In a post to X, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk told Carr that his praise was “much appreciated.”.

“This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk noted.

It has been revealed that proponents of solar-powered orbital data centers say such constellations will address the top concerns about terrestrial data centers, including land use, power consumption and water requirements for cooling. Critics point to the engineering challenges, including concerns about cooling the satellites, managing space traffic and dealing with orbital debris.

In approving SpaceX’s application, the FCC rejected opposition from Amazon and Viasat, as well as from the American Astronomical Society, which raised concerns about the constellation’s impact on the night sky. The AAS said in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision.

The FCC attached several conditions to its authorization, including requirements for communications backups, regular updates and a detailed initiative for orbital debris mitigation.

SpaceX was cleared to operate its satellites at orbits ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (310 to 623 miles) in altitude. The first satellite is to be put into operation no later than 2033, and the FCC calls for the full constellation to be operating by 2040.

It has been revealed that in August, SpaceX announced that it was partnering with Nvidia to design the compute payload for the Starmind AI1 satellite. “Each of the Starmind satellites will include Nvidia Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs for datacenter-class space compute,” SpaceX said at the time.

SpaceX’s facility in Redmond, Wash., makes the satellites for the Starlink telecommunications network — but in a filing related to this year’s initial public offering, SpaceX stated its operation in Bastrop, Texas, would be put in charge of producing AI compute satellites.

The FCC said it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals and intends to problem decisions on each proposal “according to the agency’s regular procedures.”.

Recent findings suggest that on Monday, XRP briefly rose above $1 after the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia sparked a rally on Wall Street and a wave of short liquidations in the crypto market. At the peak of the move, short liquidations on XRP exceeded long liquidations by 578%, according to CoinGlass data.

On the XRPUSDT perpetual contract on Binance, the price of XRP went from $0.94 to as high as $1.02 within minutes after 14:00 UTC, and later it pulled back and stood at $0.984, according to TradingView.

In a recent development, earlier on Monday, before the opening bell, Nvidia announced that its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately. The tech giant mentioned that the board was satisfied with Huang's "candor and ability to lead" after a series of meetings with him, and that its independent investigation would continue. According to the company, the board received input from senior U.S. government officials and concluded that Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk.".

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones mentioned in a statement.

Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and on Nov. 17, during the organization's earnings call, Jones mentioned that the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.".

In premarket trading, Nvidia stock jumped 27% to $159.48 as of 9 a.m. ET, and at the start of U.S. trading on Monday, Nvidia shares were up more than 30%. The rally spread across Wall Street, and the S&P 500 rose as much as 5.6% and the Nasdaq 100 as much as 7.9%, according to NBC News.

In a recent development, coinGlass data reveals that $9.45 million worth of XRP positions were liquidated over the past 24 hours, and $7.18 million of that amount came from short positions. Long positions accounted for $2.27 million.

Recent findings suggest that the same happened across the rest of the crypto market. In total, 110,663 traders were liquidated for $660.89 million over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGlass, and shorts accounted for $515.94 million of that amount.

Bitcoin led the list with $273.26 million in liquidations, and 82.8% of that amount came from short positions. Ethereum followed with $139.07 million, and Solana was third with $24.93 million.

Besides, perpetual contracts on Nvidia stock and on SOXL, a triple-leveraged exchange-traded fund on semiconductor stocks, were next on the list with $16.34 million and $15.01 million in liquidations, respectively, according to CoinGlass.

Island is a fresh screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time.
  • This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.
  • Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a massive mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

According to recent reports, “So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”.

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

In a recent development, “A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.

In a recent development, what’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping customers meet their goals, the startup’s early data demonstrates. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into consumers’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

In a recent development, the idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active consumers-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

Sources indicate that the app is right now free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The firm hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

Industry observers note that some video games exist at the confluence point between a surprising number of genres, which can make them difficult to explain to people who aren’t hip-deep in the hobby. That’s why several of the most popular categories are currently nicknamed after the most visible games in them, such as the “Metroidvania” or “Soulslike.” Sure, this isn’t anywhere near the biggest problem in the video game industry at the moment, but we’re going to have to figure this out sooner or later.

In a recent development, aether & Iron, created by the Issaquah, Wash.-based developer Seismic Squirrel, with co-developer Chaos Theory Games, is at one of those weird genre points. It’s described by its developers as a “narrative RPG,” which works well enough, but that also doesn’t exactly say that much.

Industry observers note that it’s worth saying up front that Aether & Iron is on a slow boil. It’s a 30-hour game that unfolds at a careful pace, building out an elaborate science-fiction setting from first principles. If you’re looking for fast thrills, it’s not the experience for you. Instead, think of it like a long novel with points of potential failure, where every opportunity for interactivity is also a chance for you to take its story in a different direction.

Industry observers note that aether & Iron is set in an alternate universe where a strange substance called aether was found beneath Manhattan in 1871. Sixty-seven years later, the study and exploitation of aether has become its own branch of science, which led to a great technological leap forward. Much of New York has been transformed into a three-tiered flying city, split between the Lowers, the Uppers and the Heights. The higher a neighborhood flies, the higher its society.

You enter the story in 1938 in the role of Gia Randazzo, a smuggler from the Lowers who’s hit hard times. She’s so desperate for work that she takes a job she shouldn’t, as a driver and bodyguard for a young scientist from the Heights named Eleanor Reinhardt. It should be a milk run, but Dr. Reinhardt has enemies she doesn’t know about.

In short order, an assassin tries to kill them both, someone steals Gia’s car, and she and Dr. Reinhardt end up stuck together in the worst parts of the Lowers. With no money, a loaner vehicle and few friends left, Gia has to figure out who wants Dr. Reinhardt dead and why. That puts her on a collision course with a revolutionary movement, several of Latest York’s power brokers and a conspiracy that could knock the city back out of the sky.

You could call Aether & Iron something like “airship noir.” Despite its science-fiction trappings, it’s a dark detective novel at heart. Yes, humanity’s built up into the sky, but the street is always the street. Mickey Spillane meets William Gibson.

During dialogue and investigation sequences, Aether & Iron uses a pair of virtual six-sided dice to determine whether you succeed or fail at a given task. As you get further into the game, you can acquire items that let you reroll those dice on a failed check.

In a recent development, more importantly, you earn experience points for accomplishments and victories, which grant you skill points that can be spent in one of nine categories. You can customize Gia to follow several distinct character tracks, such as a detective, a back-alley brawler or a fast-talking con woman. That influences the path you take through the game and the options that become available to you.

In a recent development, no matter how you choose to play Gia, you can’t always avoid a fight. All the combat in Aether & Iron takes place behind the wheel, with Gia and her crew driving customized vehicles. You can acquire a whole fleet of cars and trucks, then kit them out with special weapons, utility devices, armored plates and matching paint jobs.

Recent findings suggest that each fight consists of a turn-based tactical battle through the streets in and around New York. In addition to simply shooting up an enemy, you can sideswipe them to force them off the road or into other cars.

Many of the city’s thoroughfares are falling apart or prone to sudden lane changes, so most fights will have their own set of additional hazards. Fortunately, they’re as dangerous to your enemies as they are to you, so you can exploit the road hazards if you think fast enough.

In a recent development, if I had to point at one problem I’ve got with Aether & Iron, it might be that the combat has a couple of unlabeled difficulty curves. Specifically, a few fights are built around specific types of damage to such a degree that the only real way past them is to reload an old save and modify all my vehicles for that particular encounter.

Industry observers note that if you like the idea of constantly tweaking your vehicle collection for specific combat purposes, like heat shielding or knockback resistance, you’ll have some fun here. If you’re like me and you tend to rely on set-and-forget general-purpose builds, you’ll run into some roadblocks.

According to recent reports, other than that, you might know already whether or not you want to check it out. There’s a lot of care and art in Aether & Iron, mixed with a unique science-fiction setting that isn’t quite like anything else in video games at the moment.

It has been revealed that aether & Iron is currently available for PC and Mac via Steam for $24.99. Seismic Squirrel plans to release the game for PlayStation and Xbox in 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines.
  • Recent findings suggest that so far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows.
  • Industry observers note that to get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans.

Recent findings suggest that so far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

Industry observers note that to get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.

Much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.

As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.

Recent findings suggest that by far the largest funding recipient is Mercor, a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old organization raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.

Sources indicate that san Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor claims it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.

In a recent development, the next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob, a Latest York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce1-led financing.

According to recent reports, of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.

In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox, an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old firm picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.

According to recent reports, agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview, a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI, which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.

Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform, confirmed a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.

So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?

Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.

Overall, the bulk of substantial rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.

Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual firm highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.

ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1332 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

It has been revealed that that detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no upcoming mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain claims nothing moves unless it passes.

Industry observers note that if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's new private AI app, ZetaLabs, rolls out alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a upcoming whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

It has been revealed that holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

In a recent development, two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

In a recent development, on Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

According to recent reports, that sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain states it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain indicates the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

According to recent reports, scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

Sources indicate that on the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

Sources indicate that the vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement strategy for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States Department of Justice (DOJ) has initiated a significant legal push to address the theft of over $6 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance by North Korean hackers last month.

In a recent development, as per a Nov. 23 announcement, the DOJ noted that it has filed a civil forfeiture complaint to recover over $1.1 billion worth of stolen cryptocurrency as part of its efforts to retrieve the billions lost in the massive hack.

Industry observers note that the recent development comes less than a month after North Korean hackers reportedly broke into Binance on Oct. 29 in one of the biggest crypto heists ever.

The DOJ claimed that its recent civil forfeiture action focuses on over $1.1 billion worth of USD Coin (USDC), a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to the U.S. dollar and issued by Circle.

The assets are alleged to have been stolen from Binance and laundered by North Korean cybercriminals.

In a recent development, significantly, the assets had previously been frozen under a restraining order obtained by the government earlier this month. With the fresh court filing, the potential recovery of the assets has taken another step forward.

The DOJ further claimed that U.S. authorities have successfully helped freeze, seize or return over $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency since the attack in October.

This is nearly half of the total $6 billion-plus stolen from Binance, though the government did not provide details about how much of that has been returned to the exchange.

In a recent development, the importance of collaboration between law enforcement agencies and crypto firms to ensure that hackers don't get away with stolen assets was stressed by Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva.

Industry observers note that “North Korean cyber hackers stole over $6 billion of cryptocurrency from Binance. But prompt coordination with both the government and our private sector partners helped to avoid the bulk of these assets from being lost,” Duva mentioned.

According to recent reports, U.S. authorities have further revealed the sophisticated money laundering techniques used by North Korean hackers to conceal their stolen cryptocurrency.

FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman noted that the regime uses intricate money laundering methods to convert stolen digital assets into funds for its illicit activities.

After the Binance hack, authorities quickly worked to trace the stolen funds and coordinate with crypto service providers to block further transfers.

The U.S. Secret Service claimed that its investigators were able to detect and freeze some of the stolen funds within minutes of the hack.

Sources indicate that "The bad actors in this intrusion thought they could run from law enforcement. They've found out they were wrong," said Secret Service Special Agent in Charge Todd Bratz.
